title: DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models
research_question: Can dynamic RAG improve knowledge-intensive generation by deciding both when to retrieve and what to retrieve from the LLM's real-time information needs rather than from fixed retrieval schedules or only the most recent generated text?
methodology: DRAGIN combines Real-time Information Needs Detection (RIND), which scores generated tokens using uncertainty, semantic importance, and influence on later tokens, with Query Formulation based on Self-attention (QFS), which selects information-relevant tokens from the broader generation context for retrieval. The framework is training-free and is evaluated with multiple LLMs on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, StrategyQA, and IIRC using Wikipedia passages and primarily BM25 retrieval. Comparisons include no-RAG, single-round RAG, fixed-length retrieval, fixed-sentence retrieval, and FLARE, with ablations isolating retrieval timing and query formulation.

key_findings.finding: DRAGIN achieved the strongest overall performance across most evaluated LLM and dataset combinations, with especially pronounced gains on multi-hop QA tasks.
key_findings.section: 5.1 Overall Results of DRAGIN and Baselines

key_findings.finding: Fixed-interval and fixed-sentence dynamic retrieval did not consistently outperform single-round RAG, supporting the claim that retrieving at an inappropriate generation point can be unhelpful.
key_findings.section: 5.1 Overall Results of DRAGIN and Baselines

key_findings.finding: When query formulation was held fixed, the RIND retrieval-timing strategy outperformed the timing strategies of FLARE, fixed-length RAG, and fixed-sentence RAG on the IIRC experiments.

When retrieval timing was held to RIND, QFS outperformed query formulations based on the last sentence, local token windows, FLARE's filtered sentence, and the complete generation context on HotpotQA.
DRAGIN required fewer retrieval calls than fixed-length and fixed-sentence RAG in the reported efficiency comparison, although FLARE generally made the fewest retrieval calls.
HotpotQA performance remained relatively stable over a broad range of RIND thresholds, while the threshold controlled how frequently retrieval was activated.
BM25 outperformed the SGPT dense retriever in all three reported DRAGIN retriever comparisons on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, and IIRC.

limitations: RIND and QFS require access to Transformer self-attention information, making the method unusable with APIs that do not expose the required internals.
The experiments focus on four knowledge-intensive QA and reasoning benchmarks rather than long-lived workplace communication or heterogeneous enterprise evidence.
The external corpus is Wikipedia segmented into fixed-size passages, so document permissions, revisions, source versions, and enterprise access-control constraints are not modeled.
Retrieval stopping is driven by repeated information-need detection rather than an explicit global evidence-completeness criterion.
The evaluation primarily measures answer correctness and retrieval-call counts rather than end-to-end monetary cost, temporal validity, or evidence provenance.
raw_claims: DRAGIN makes separate decisions about when retrieval is needed and what query should be issued.
RIND uses generation uncertainty together with token importance and influence to detect information needs.
QFS uses self-attention over the generation context to choose tokens for the retrieval query.
The framework does not require additional model training or fine-tuning.
The evaluation covers four knowledge-intensive generation benchmarks.
Single-round RAG consistently improves over direct generation in the reported experiments.
Fixed-rule dynamic retrieval does not consistently improve over single-round retrieval.
DRAGIN's retrieval-timing method performs better than the compared timing strategies in the timing ablation.
QFS performs better than the compared query-formulation strategies in the query ablation.
The full generated context is not necessarily an optimal retrieval query because it can contain redundant information.
DRAGIN usually makes fewer retrieval calls than fixed-length and fixed-sentence dynamic RAG.
The authors released code, data, and models for the work.
The method cannot directly support APIs that hide the self-attention scores it needs.
